topic.title: Mixture Models and Latent Population Structure
topic.overview: Mixture models describe a distribution as a combination of simpler components, allowing heterogeneous populations to be represented without forcing one global shape. Learning must determine component parameters, mixing weights, and sometimes the number of components. Missing or quantized observations add further ambiguity.
topic.whyItMatters: An apparent cluster can depend strongly on the assumed component family and optimization procedure. Useful methods need both computational strategies and conditions explaining when the latent structure is identifiable or reliably approximated.
topic.evolution: Early representatives use expectation-maximization for incomplete data and diagnostic mixtures. Later work develops mixture hierarchies and analyzes optimization in Gaussian mixtures. Recent approaches connect diffusion objectives, semidefinite relaxations, and moment-based distribution approximation. This expands the inference tools available, while global guarantees remain conditional on properties such as parameter constraints and rank conditions.
openQuestions: When do finite moments determine a useful mixing distribution?
How can model selection avoid adding components that merely absorb noise or missing-data artifacts?
